sessions.notes:
- Star/fork/other repo metrics live ONLY as free text in `deps_dev_v1_project_info."Project_Information"`, never as separate numeric columns. Extract the `owner/repo` slug from that text with a regex like `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, lowercase it, and join to lowercased `deps_dev_v1_project_packageversion."ProjectName"`. Don't match Project_Information to ProjectName via LIKE/substring on the whole text blob.
- Fork counts appear in three mutually exclusive phrasings that together cover every row: a "count of N forks" style, a "forked N times" style, and a plain "N forks" style. Try all three (case-insensitive) before trusting one, strip thousands commas, cast to a number. Star counts and other metrics likely have similarly varied phrasings worth surveying first.
- `Licenses` and `VersionInfo` columns are JSON stored as text, sometimes pretty-printed across lines. Parse as JSON rather than substring/LIKE, which can miss whitespace variants.
- One GitHub project maps to many package versions in project_packageversion. To pick "the" version for a project, rank by most recent publish time, then release ordinal, then version string, and take the top-ranked one per project.
- Join path: packageinfo(System,Name,Version) = project_packageversion(System,Name,Version); project_packageversion.ProjectName equals the slug extracted from project_info.Project_Information, not a free-text search match.
sessions.rationale: Targets the join-differs failure on deps_dev_v1/2: the agent matched project_info to ProjectName via LIKE on raw text and used only one fork-count regex, missing rows covered by other phrasings; it also used LIKE on JSON-like Licenses/VersionInfo text and didn't select one representative latest-release version per project. Notes generalize the correct slug-extraction join key, surveying all text phrasings for numeric metrics, JSON parsing over LIKE, and per-project version selection.

sessions.notes:
- Join key: business_id values look like "businessid_N" in yelp_business; business_ref values look like "businessref_N" in yelp_review/yelp_tip, same N. Join by matching the numeric suffix after stripping each prefix, not raw string comparison.
- State: yelp_business.description always has "..., <City>, <ST>," (two-letter uppercase state) after the city. Use a word-boundary regex so trailing punctuation isn't captured. Some codes are non-US (e.g. Canadian provinces); for "U.S. state" questions, filter against the 50 US codes + DC.
- Categories aren't a column. description = "<varying lead-in: Located at/Situated at/Located in/This vibrant spot at/This <city>,<ST> location> ... <City>, <ST>, <descriptor> offers ... <category>, <category>...". Lead-in wording varies across rows. To get categories, take the text after "<City>, <ST>," and pull capitalized phrase(s) joined by ", "/" & "/"/"/" of "/parenthetical qualifiers. Don't anchor on one fixed lead-in or ending phrase; it only covers some rows.
- yelp_review.date/yelp_tip.date mix three text formats in one column: 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS', 'DD Mon YYYY, HH24:MI', 'Month DD, YYYY at HH12:MI AM'. Detect each row's shape and parse with the matching to_timestamp format; one LIKE/regex alone misses rows in other shapes.
- "Average rating of businesses in <group>" means pool all matching reviews into one AVG, not average of per-business averages.
- Break ties in "highest/most" with a secondary sort key, not arbitrary LIMIT 1 order.
sessions.rationale: Targets yelp/2 (state regex lacked word boundary, no US-state filter, wrong join column, pooled-vs-per-business averaging) and yelp/6 (category extraction anchored on a single fixed phrase instead of the general post-location pattern; date parsing missed the three mixed formats). Also documents the correct join-key relationship and tie-break practice to protect currently-passing queries.

- Join key: `yelp_business.business_id` = `businessid_N`; `yelp_review.business_ref` / `yelp_tip.business_ref` = `businessref_N` (same N). Join with `replace(business_id,'businessid_','businessref_') = business_ref` (or the reverse), not by string-comparing prefixes directly.
- State code: `yelp_business.description` always contains "..., <City>, <ST>," (two-letter uppercase state). Extract with a word-boundary regex like `substring(description from ', ([A-Z]{2})\M')` so it doesn't also grab trailing punctuation. Some codes are non-US (e.g. Canadian provinces like 'AB'); when a question says "U.S. state", filter the extracted code against the list of 50 US state codes + DC before aggregating.
- Categories are NOT a separate column: description = "Located at <addr> in <City>, <ST>, this <facility/establishment/...> offers ... <category>, <category>, ...". A few lead-in templates exist ("Located at...", "Situated at...", "Located in...", "This vibrant spot at...", "This <city>, <ST> location..."). To get categories, take everything in the description AFTER the "<City>, <ST>," clause, then split/extract the capitalized phrase(s) joined by ", ", " & ", "/", " of ", or "(New)"-style qualifiers — do not use a fixed phrase like "featuring ... perfect" as the boundary, it only matches some rows.
- `yelp_review.date` and `yelp_tip.date` are text in three distinct formats mixed in the same column (survey before parsing): `'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'`, `'DD Mon YYYY, HH24:MI'` (e.g. '31 Dec 2018, 00:15'), and `'Month DD, YYYY at HH12:MI AM'`. Parse each with `to_timestamp` using the matching format per row (branch with `CASE`/regex on shape), rather than pattern-matching substrings like '2016' or a single date format — a LIKE '%2016%' or single-format regex will silently miss rows in the other formats.
- When averaging a rating "of businesses in <group>", compute it as one AVG over all matching reviews pooled together (not an average of per-business averages), unless the question explicitly asks for a per-business figure.
- Ties in "highest/most" rankings should break deterministically (e.g. by a secondary count, then by id) — do not rely on arbitrary row order from LIMIT 1.

sessions.notes:
You answer one question about one dataset by writing SQL.

## The data

Every table in the Tables list is loaded into one Postgres 16 schema and named `<dataset>_<table>`. The database description below was written for the original stores (SQLite, DuckDB, MongoDB): ignore the storage format, use the Postgres names from the Tables list, and write Postgres SQL. Quote mixed-case columns (`"Name"`).

## How to work

1. Read the description and the hints. Map every part of the question to a table and a column before you query.
2. Explore with small queries (`LIMIT`, counts, distinct values); `describe_table` gives a table's types, null rates and top values in one call. Free text is generated from a few templates: survey a column's phrasings over the whole table and count what your pattern reads before you trust it.
3. Build the answer as ONE SQL statement. Use CTEs for steps; regex (`substring(s from 'p')`, `regexp_match`, `split_part`) for text; `to_timestamp` for dates stored as text; joins on exact keys, never `ILIKE '%x%'` where a key can be extracted. Read literally: "more than" is strict. Rankings need a tie-break (add a secondary/ascending-id sort key, don't rely on arbitrary LIMIT order).
4. Join keys often aren't directly equal: one side may carry a prefix/suffix (e.g. `id_123` vs `ref_123`), leading/stray characters (`#`, whitespace), or different casing. Extract the comparable part (numeric suffix, `ltrim(trim(x),'#')`, `lower()`) on both sides and compare that, never raw string/number equality across differently-formatted keys.
5. A single date/timestamp-as-text column can mix several distinct formats across rows (e.g. `'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'`, `'DD Mon YYYY, HH24:MI'`, `'Month DD, YYYY at HH12:MI AM'`). Detect each row's shape (regex/length) and parse with the matching format; one `to_timestamp`/cast or one regex alone silently drops or misparses rows in other shapes.
6. When a question asks to list entities "with" some attribute(s) (count, date, name...), return those attribute columns too, not just the identifying column.
7. Finish with `submit_answer(sql, mode, answer, step)`:
   - `sql`: the final statement. Its result must contain the answer.
   - mode `pass_through` (prefer it): the answer IS that result; the harness re-runs `sql` and renders it. Name the columns as the question names them, and return only what the question asks for.
   - mode `derived`: the answer needs one step after the SQL (reading the returned text to reach a verdict, choosing between returned rows). Give the answer, values only, and describe the step in one line.

If the SQL fails or returns no rows when re-run, `submit_answer` says so: fix it and submit again. Call it once it succeeds, then stop.
sessions.rationale: Added two recurring cross-dataset lessons to system.md: (1) join keys frequently need extraction/normalization (numeric suffix, stripped prefix, case) rather than raw equality, seen in crmarenapro, bookreview, yelp, music_brainz_20k, deps_dev_v1 — this maps to the largest failure categories (join differs, wrong tables) across 7+ datasets; (2) a single date/text column can mix multiple distinct formats requiring per-row detection, seen explicitly in bookreview, googlelocal, yelp, stockmarket, patents. Also generalized the tie-break note (crmarenapro, yelp) and added a line about returning requested attribute columns, not just an identifying column (github_repos, generalizes 'return only what the question asks for'). Left dataset-specific notes untouched; no question text or answer values included.
